subject: Spatial Surveys, Royle and Nichols Abundance-Occupancy Model

messages.author: 0c69c6d399345fab
messages.subject: Spatial Surveys, Royle and Nichols Abundance-Occupancy Model
parts:
Hi unmarkers,

Quick question. Working through a revision here, and a reviewer wants to me to check to see if count data may have
skewed my modelling results when using the single-species season model (MacKenzie et al. 2002). I used PRESENCE to produce these models. Anyways, I am considering using Royle's 2003 which uses count data to acount for heterogeneous detection probabilities associated with variation in abundance across sites. Normally, I wouldn't think twice about this (after all, that's what this model was designed for!). However, my data was not collected temporally; individual surveys in this study represent spatial subunits within a site.  Therefore, I'm assuming this would be an inappropriate way to approximate psi, or examine covariate relationships. Thoughts?


Sincerely,

Josh

messages.author: 4a635fe980c8c1cd
messages.subject: Re: Spatial Surveys, Royle and Nichols Abundance-Occupancy Model
parts:
Just my $0.02: if you can assume the spatial replicates operate independently (something like Figure 1 in the Tigers on Trails paper by Hines et al. 2010) both the standard occupancy model and the RN model should work fine (also assuming the other implicit/parametric assumptions are met). Abundance might well induce more heterogeneity in detection across spatial replicates than temporal replicates in certain situations. If there's some reason to suspect serial correlation in observations or other dependence, the Hines 2010 model might be appropriate, or if you can figure out how to fit it, you could consider the approach from this paper which is kind of the RN analogue (https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/j.2041-210X.2011.00159.x). 

W/r/t counts, not quite sure what you mean--or maybe not sure what the reviewer means. Presumably you've reduced the counts to 0/1 when fitting the occupancy model. Maybe a majority of studies that estimate occupancy collapse some sort of count of observations within a temporal interval (e.g., trail cameras, bird point counts, etc.)?

Cheers,

John
